<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Narjes Nourzad
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Southern California
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Electrical and Computer Engineering
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Los Angeles, CA 90007, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">nourzad@usc.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Carlee Joe-Wong
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Carnegie Mellon University
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Electrical and Computer Engineering
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">cjoewong@andrew.cmu.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often face high sample complexity in sparse or delayed reward settings, due to limited prior knowledge.
Conversely, large language models (LLMs) can provide subgoal structures, plausible trajectories, and abstract priors that support early learning.
Yet heavy reliance on LLMs introduces scalability issues and risks dependence on unreliable signals, motivating ongoing efforts to integrate LLM guidance without compromising RL’s autonomy.
We propose MIRA (<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">M</span>emory-<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">I</span>ntegrated <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">R</span>einforcement Learning <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">A</span>gent), <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">which incorporates a structured, evolving <span id="abstract1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory graph</span> to guide early learning.</span>
This graph stores decision-relevant information, such as trajectory segments and subgoal decompositions, and is co-constructed from the agent’s high-return experiences and LLM outputs, <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">amortizing LLM queries into a persistent memory instead of relying on continuous real-time supervision.</span>
From this structure, we derive a <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">utility</span> signal that <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">softly adjusts</span> advantage estimation to refine policy updates without altering the underlying reward function.
As training progresses, the agent’s policy surpasses the initial LLM-derived priors, and the utility term decays, leaving long-term convergence guarantees intact.
<span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We show theoretically that this utility-based shaping improves early-stage learning in sparse-reward settings.</span>
Empirically, MIRA outperforms RL baselines and <span id="abstract1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">reaches returns comparable to methods that rely on frequent LLM supervision,</span> while requiring substantially fewer online LLM queries<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
        Project webpage : <a href="https://narjesno.github.io/MIRA/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://narjesno.github.io/MIRA/</a></span></span></span>.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning (RL) models sequential decision-making as interactions with an environment and learns behavior from reward-driven feedback.
RL has achieved strong results in domains including robotic manipulation, dynamic scheduling, and autonomous planning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nourzad et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, these advances often rely on environments with dense, readily accessible rewards.
In many tasks, rewards are sparse or delayed, appearing only when specific goals are reached or several steps after the action unfolds.
These weak or infrequent rewards obscure which past actions influenced the outcome, making it difficult to credit the eventual reward appropriately <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Velu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
This uncertainty weakens the gradient signal, leaving policy updates underinformed. Thus, agents become highly data-hungry and require large numbers of interactions to learn useful behaviors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devidze et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
These challenges intensify under partial observability, as agents must generalize from limited state information and often struggle early in training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hausknecht and Stone, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kurniawati, 2022</a>)</cite>.
In such settings, random exploration rarely uncovers informative trajectories, leading to slow convergence and high variance in returns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) provide a complementary source of prior knowledge, especially in environments where rewards are sparse, feedback is delayed, and observations are partial.
They have demonstrated capabilities in reasoning over abstract goals, interpreting high-level intent, and leveraging broad prior knowledge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These properties make them natural candidates for providing structured guidance for RL agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schoepp et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A growing body of work has explored how pretrained LLMs can support RL to improve sample efficiency. One line of research positions the LLM as an implicit or explicit reward model, either estimating reward signals from environment descriptions or generating code to define reward functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rocamonde et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhambri et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Another line leverages LLMs to generate high-level plans, policy sketches, or step-by-step guidance during training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu and Sadigh, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dasgupta et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. A third direction focuses on task-level guidance such as subgoal decomposition, curriculum design, or goal interpretation from natural language <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn and others, 2023</a>)</cite>. Additional related approaches appear in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Related Works ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Research challenges.</span>
The existing approaches, although promising, typically require <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">frequent (often per-step) LLM supervision</span>, making the agent’s performance heavily reliant on LLM inference, which introduces several difficulties.
First, it can interfere with the RL learning signal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">limiting autonomous decision-making and reducing the agent’s ability to generalize or adapt if the LLM becomes unavailable.</span>
Second, since LLMs cannot interact directly with the environment or gather real-time feedback, full reliance on their instructions is suboptimal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and dilutes environment-driven feedback. Indeed, LLMs carry fundamental risks such as hallucinated outputs, prompt sensitivity, and limited grounding in physical environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tonmoy et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, making their outputs potentially unreliable.
Frequent queries also raise scalability concerns due to computational cost and latency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib105" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib100" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Still, relying solely on RL ignores the structured knowledge encoded in LLMs that could accelerate learning or shape behavior in meaningful ways.
<span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Thus, the fundamental challenge <span id="S1.p3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">lies in incorporating LLM guidance in a way that leverages its complementary benefits while preserving the optimization dynamics that make RL effective.</span></span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/paper_mira_whole.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/184;" width="548" height="184" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#7A7A7A;">Offline</span> priors and <span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#E2B3C3;">online</span> LLM suggestions are filtered by a <span id="S1.F1.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#AAADBA;">screening unit</span> before being incorporated into the memory graph as <em id="S1.F1.11" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#80A970;">healthy grafts</em>. <span id="S1.F1.12" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;">MIRA</span> agent acts under partial observations, interacting with the environment. A utility module evaluates trajectory rollouts against the evolving <span id="S1.F1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#E2B3C3;">memory graph</span>, producing a utility signal that shapes advantage estimation and policy updates.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Our contributions.</span> In this work, we propose MIRA (<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">M</span>emory-<span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">I</span>ntegrated <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">R</span>einforcement Learning <span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">A</span>gent), a method that integrates LLM-derived guidance into reinforcement learning through a structured <span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory graph</span>.
The memory graph provides an evolving representation of task-relevant information, co-constructed from the agent’s experience and LLM outputs.
<span id="S1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Offline priors initialize the structure, while infrequent online queries on batches of partial observations can further refine it during training.</span>
Nodes represent decision-relevant context, such as trajectory segments, and edges encode the hierarchical decomposition linking goals to their subgoals.
The graph is designed to remain compact, adding minimal overhead relative to standard replay buffers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib106" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schaul et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.
The memory graph allows the agent to organize and reuse information <span id="S1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without repeated LLM queries</span>, providing a persistent source of structured knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">O<span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">ver time, the agent validates, revises, and extends the structure based on its own experience, improving beyond what LLM guidance alone can provide and filtering out mistaken online suggestions.</span>
The resulting graph limits dependence on real-time LLM access, alleviating concerns about latency, query cost, and scalability.
To integrate the LLM-derived information into learning, we derive a <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">utility signal</span> from the memory graph and use it to softly shape advantage estimates in each RL iteration.
<span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This signal guides early rollouts by reinforcing reward-driven gradients when aligned and moderating updates that arise from an inaccurate critic, helping the agent explore more effectively in sparse-reward settings without overriding the environment’s feedback.</span>
Theoretically, we show that the utility term accelerates early learning.
As the policy improves and surpasses the usefulness of LLM-derived guidance, the shaping influence fades, ensuring convergence in the long-horizon limit.
We empirically evaluate the effectiveness, sample efficiency, and overhead of incorporating LLM guidance across multiple benchmark environments. 

<br class="ltx_break">Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">A memory-integrated framework for LLM guidance:</span><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">
We propose <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MIRA</span>, a reinforcement learning agent that integrates LLM-derived guidance through a memory graph co-constructed </span><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">from agent experience and offline or infrequent online LLM outputs. The graph evolves throughout training, reducing reliance on real-time LLM queries.</span><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Utility-based advantage shaping:</span><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
We introduce </span><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">utility-shaped advantage estimation</span><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, which incorporates graph-derived utility into advantage computation</span><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text"> without architectural changes and is compatible with any advantage-based policy-gradient method.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Convergence-compatible shaping:</span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">
We provide </span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">theoretical guarantees</span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> showing that by decaying the shaping influence as the policy improves</span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">, we preserve long-horizon convergence properties of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017a</a>)</cite> </span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">and correct any inaccuracies in LLM outputs</span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text">.</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Empirical validation across benchmarks:</span><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">
We demonstrate <span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">empirically</span> that MIRA improves sample efficiency over RL and hierarchical baselines and reaches final performance comparable to methods requiring continuous LLM supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhambri et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, while using far fewer online queries.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> details MIRA’s architecture; Sections <a href="#S3" title="3 Experimental Setup ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4" title="4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> present experimental setup and results across multiple benchmarks; and Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Conclusion and Future Work ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> concludes with a discussion of our findings and possible directions for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the design of MIRA, whose development is guided by two desiderata: <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">(i)</span> improve early learning by incorporating task-relevant priors from an LLM,
<span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">(ii)</span> minimize reliance on continuous real-time LLM supervision to ensure scalability and maintain autonomous policy learning.
MIRA is built on the standard policy-gradient formulation for reinforcement learning (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Background ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Memory Graph Design</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The agent maintains an evolving memory graph that organizes information drawn from both LLM suggestions and agent rollouts. Nodes of the graph represent decision-relevant context,</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:38%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/graph.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:167/113;" width="167" height="113" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">MIRA’s evolving memory graph. Trajectory segments <math id="S2.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">τ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> are grouped under subgoal nodes <math id="S2.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">κ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. Subgoals can be shared across multiple final goals, enabling reuse of common behaviors.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">and edges encode the hierarchical decomposition of goals into subgoals as provided by the LLM <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.1 Memory Graph Design ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>)</span>.
This structure can be expressed as</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=\Bigl\{\big((o,a)_{\tau_{j}},\zeta_{j},\hat{r}_{j}\big)_{c_{j}}\Bigr\}_{j=1}^{N}\;\cup\;\bigl\{\kappa_{\ell}\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\;\cup\;\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.502em">∪</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.502em">∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=\Bigl\{\big((o,a)_{\tau_{j}},\zeta_{j},\hat{r}_{j}\big)_{c_{j}}\Bigr\}_{j=1}^{N}\;\cup\;\bigl\{\kappa_{\ell}\bigr\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\;\cup\;\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Each trajectory node <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> consists of a partial observation <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{\tau_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{\tau_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math> and an action <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\tau_{j}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\tau_{j}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
It is also associated with a goal term <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta_{j}\in\{\textsl{g}_{j},\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta_{j}\in\{\textsl{g}_{j},\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicating either a final goal <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\textsl{g}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\textsl{g}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> or an abstract subgoal <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mi>j</mi></msub></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\kappa_{\ell}^{\textsl{g}_{j}})</annotation></semantics></math> that the trajectory is intended to complete.
In addition, the node stores an estimated (sub)goal reward <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> for the action sequence, reflecting progress toward completing its associated subgoal, and a confidence score <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> derived from the LLM-derived statistics.
The second set of nodes <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\kappa_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\kappa_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> represents subgoals <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> provided by the LLM from the environment description.
The final term <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}\}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the agent’s target goal(s).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The graph is initialized with offline LLM priors and evolves as training progresses.
Nodes are added or updated when the agent <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">produces trajectory segments that either introduce a novel segment for a known (sub)goal or achieve a higher estimated return than the existing entry for the same (sub)goal.</span>
Existing nodes can also be updated when the agent’s experience strengthens entries that were initially derived from low-confidence LLM outputs.
Online LLM suggestions may also be added as new nodes when available, provided they pass screening; <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">an online query is triggered only when the rollout utility signal remains near zero for several consecutive episodes, indicating that the current graph offers no helpful guidance. In such cases, the current policy is either exploring regions unsupported by the memory graph or that the graph itself is missing useful segments. </span>
Nodes are pruned when they remain unused for a fixed horizon of episodes. <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Each node maintains an access counter updated whenever it contributes to the utility; nodes whose counters do not change within this window are removed</span>, reflecting reduced relevance to recent rollouts.
Offline LLM nodes, though generally stable, may also be removed when rendered obsolete.
<span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Additional details about graph construction and environment-specific examples are given in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Memory Graph Construction Details ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</span>
<span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This process keeps the graph compact and adaptive, while ensuring that any low-quality or misleading prior segments naturally fade as higher-return agent-generated trajectories replace them or lead to their pruning.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Offline and Online Guidance</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MIRA incorporates two complementary forms of LLM guidance, accessed either <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">offline</span> prior to training or <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">online</span> during training.
Offline outputs are <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">generated using full access to the task description, providing trajectory segments and subgoal decompositions that initialize the memory graph with structured priors. </span>
Offline nodes accelerate early exploration and remain a persistent baseline source of guidance that complements the adaptive updates introduced by online LLM queries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Online suggestions are incorporated during training when the agent fails to obtain useful guidance <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(i.e., when the rollout utility remains near zero)</span> from its memory graph for several consecutive episodes.
The LLM is constrained to the same partial observability as the agent and, when triggered, may return plans that correspond to short trajectories.
Alternatively, it may provide control signals that bias the action preferences over an extended horizon until the current task segment is completed.
All online outputs are passed through the <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Screening Unit</span>, which discards low-confidence suggestions.
Accepted plans are grafted into the memory graph as new trajectory segments, while accepted control signals bias the policy through soft logit injection, i.e., adding a bounded penalty to the logits of discouraged actions. <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This penalty induces only a soft preference before the softmax and cannot collapse the action distribution. PPO’s clipped objective controls the update size, ensuring that the injected bias functions as lightweight guidance that the critic can override when it strongly disagrees with the value estimates</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biza et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">Screening Unit.</span>
To ensure reliability, online outputs are passed through a lightweight <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Screening Unit</span> designed to reduce hallucinations and reasoning failures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Confidence is estimated in two complementary ways.
When token-level likelihoods are available, <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">we compute the geometric mean of the per-token probabilities of the completion as a confidence measure</span>.
When such likelihoods are unavailable or incomplete (e.g., only top-k likelihoods are provided), we instead estimate confidence by sampling multiple independent completions <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">and measuring agreement across them. A majority-consistency test is then applied to retain only those outputs that appear reliably across the sampled completions.</span>
Suggestions that fail to meet a fixed threshold under either criterion are discarded.
While this procedure does not eliminate all high-confidence errors, it serves as an effective filter that reduces the risk of hallucinated or low-quality outputs.
The screened outputs, referred to as <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">healthy grafts</span> in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, are incorporated into the memory graph as new nodes to further help the policy learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Utility Signal Computation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Utility is defined at the level of individual state–action pairs and is computed from the same rollouts used for advantage estimation under the current policy.</span>
Each state-action in the trajectory <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=\{(o_{t},a_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=\{(o_{t},a_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is matched against the corresponding state–action pairs <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(o_{t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(o_{t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime}})</annotation></semantics></math> in the stored trajectory <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The appropriate memory node <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is selected based on the environment instance (e.g., the seed-specific layout) in that training iteration. We then compute the utility for each pair <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> as:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}\doteq c_{m}\cdot\hat{r}_{m}\cdot\rho(\textsl{g}_{\triangleright},\zeta_{m})\cdot\mathcal{s}\big((o_{t},a_{t}),(o_{t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime}})_{\tau_{m}}\big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≐</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓈</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>τ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}\doteq c_{m}\cdot\hat{r}_{m}\cdot\rho(\textsl{g}_{\triangleright},\zeta_{m})\cdot\mathcal{s}\big((o_{t},a_{t}),(o_{t^{\prime}},a_{t^{\prime}})_{\tau_{m}}\big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Steps that do not match any stored trajectory segment receive zero utility.</span>
The similarity function <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{s}(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝓈</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{s}(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> measures how closely the agent’s behavior aligns with the stored trajectory.
It incorporates both action agreement and spatial consistency, such as overlap in grid positions or directional alignment in tabular settings <span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(Algorithm <a href="#alg3" title="Algorithm 3 ‣ F.1 Similarity Score ‣ Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)</span>.
To capture semantic structure, the raw similarity score is weighted by a goal-alignment factor <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Each subgoal description specifies a target object or region and a high-level action applied to it; simple rule-based parsing yields a paired entity and action-phase token. </span> The Jaccard similarity between the entity–phase token sets extracted from the agent’s target subgoal and each memory entry defines <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. This weighting increases the influence of memory entries that share underlying entities or action phases with the target subgoal and downweights matches corresponding to unrelated parts of the task <span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(Algorithm <a href="#alg4" title="Algorithm 4 ‣ F.2 Goal Alignment ‣ Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>)</span>.
<span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Thus, a transition contributes to utility only when both its behavioral similarity and its semantic alignment with the relevant subgoal are high.</span>
Finally, the score is modulated by the confidence <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> and estimated reward <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> attached to the memory node (Algorithm <a href="#alg5" title="Algorithm 5 ‣ F.2 Goal Alignment ‣ Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
<span id="S2.SS3.p1.2.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">This formulation also helps limit the influence of incorrect LLM guidance that may have passed screening. When an LLM suggestion is inaccurate, its influence naturally diminishes: such segments typically contribute little utility since their estimated reward is low or their similarity score remains small, reflecting weak positional alignment or inconsistent action patterns between the agent’s rollout and the stored LLM-derived segment. Further details on the utility computation are presented in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Adaptive Advantage Shaping</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We incorporate memory-derived utility into the policy update by augmenting the standard advantage term.
Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.4 Adaptive Advantage Shaping ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> outlines the shaped PPO update. At iteration <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, trajectories <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{k}=\{(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t})\}</annotation></semantics></math> are collected under the policy <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The rollout batch is split into minibatches <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> for multiple gradient steps. The likelihood ratio <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> compares new and old policies, and the clip parameter <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> constrains <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> within <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1\pm\varepsilon_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>±</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1\pm\varepsilon_{k})</annotation></semantics></math> as a soft trust region.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The advantage function in policy gradient methods, denoted by <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> at a given time <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, quantifies how favorable an action <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is relative to the average action at state <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. It drives learning by reinforcing actions that have higher-than-expected returns and suppressing those that fall short.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_figure ltx_float_algorithm ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle ltx_align_floatright ltx_framed ltx_framed_top" style="width:198.7pt;">
