</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
                <math id="alg1.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}(\theta)={\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})}/{\pi_{\theta_{k}}(a_{t}|s_{t})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}(\theta)={\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})}/{\pi_{\theta_{k}}(a_{t}|s_{t})}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
                <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{\text{shaped}}(\pi_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">ℒ</mi><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">shaped</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">π</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">θ</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{\text{shaped}}(\pi_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="alg1.l8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=\mathbb{E}\left[\min(r_{t},1\!\pm\!\varepsilon_{k}){{\color[rgb]{0.7461,0.625,0.8359}\tilde{A}_{t}}}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=\mathbb{E}\left[\min(r_{t},1\!\pm\!\varepsilon_{k}){{\color[rgb]{0.7461,0.625,0.8359}\tilde{A}_{t}}}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
                <math id="alg1.l9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\leftarrow\theta+\alpha_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\leftarrow\theta+\alpha_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="alg1.l9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{\text{shaped}}(\pi_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">ℒ</mi><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">shaped</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">π</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5">θ</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#BE9FD5;" mathcolor="#BE9FD5" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{\text{shaped}}(\pi_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
               <span id="alg1.l10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l11" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
              <span id="alg1.l11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l12" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l12.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, during early training the critic is poorly calibrated due to limited exploration, often producing nearly uniform value estimates across actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Henderson et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.
As a result, the estimated advantages <math id="S2.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> provide weak learning signals, even when the agent is following behavior that is meaningfully directed toward the task.
This issue is particularly pronounced in sparse-reward settings or tasks with delayed feedback, where the critic lacks sufficient signal to distinguish between promising and unproductive behaviors.
In such cases, the estimated advantage tends to be near-zero or highly noisy for most timesteps, especially early in training (Figure <a href="#A7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ G.2 Early Advantage Dynamics ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address this, we introduce a shaped advantage as:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t},\quad 0&lt;\eta_{t}\leq 1,\;\xi_{t}\leq\delta\eta_{t},\;\delta\in[0,1),\;\lim_{t\to\infty}\eta_{t}=1,\;\lim_{t\to\infty}\xi_{t}=0." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t},\quad 0&lt;\eta_{t}\leq 1,\;\xi_{t}\leq\delta\eta_{t},\;\delta\in[0,1),\;\lim_{t\to\infty}\eta_{t}=1,\;\lim_{t\to\infty}\xi_{t}=0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">This formulation preserves the fundamental role of the advantage function, while refining it with utility-based guidance.
<span id="S2.SS4.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">It forms a cooperative process between critic predictions and the memory-derived utility.</span>
The critic provides an estimate based on learned reward prediction and bootstrapping, while the utility term injects an inductive bias derived from language-guided priors.
Together, they form a joint estimator in which each component compensates for the other’s limitations without distorting policy optimization.
When the critic signal is weak due to insufficient value discrimination, the resulting gradients are uninformative and impair the agent’s ability to bootstrap from sparse or delayed rewards.
The utility term provides additional directional guidance aligned with task objectives, accelerating learning by compensating for weak or flat gradients <span id="S2.SS4.p4.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(Figure <a href="#A7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ G.2 Early Advantage Dynamics ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>)</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As training progresses and the policy becomes more accurate, the critic’s advantage estimates <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> become more reliable.
<span id="S2.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Accordingly, the shaping weight <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ξ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is annealed to reduce the direct influence of the utility term and <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">η</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is ramped toward 1 over training.
Since the LLM-derived signals can be imperfect, annealing <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ξ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> prevents inaccuracies in those signals from being preserved in the asymptotic regime. This ensures that the final policy is optimized with respect to the true reward function <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#000000">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and remains consistent with PPO’s stability guarantees. Early in training, however, <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ξ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> remains large enough for the utility to accelerate exploration using the LLM’s possibly imperfect, but still useful, prior knowledge.
As <math id="S2.SS4.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ξ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> decays, any suboptimalities in these priors are naturally learned away, yielding the benefits of shaping during the sparse-reward phase, without biasing long-run behavior</span> or altering the policy or critic structure. See remark <a href="#A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" title="Remark (Bias–Variance Trade-off). ‣ C.4 Early-Training Advantage ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> for more explanation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Before turning to experiments, we provide an interpretive perspective on how adaptive advantage shaping affects optimization in sparse-reward regimes and in Appendix  establish that the proposed shaping mechanism preserves the policy improvement property of PPO under standard boundedness and scaling assumptions, which we formally enumerate in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>. More broadly, the method remains compatible with policy gradient algorithms that relies on advantage estimation, offering a general mechanism for integrating language-derived priors into RL.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmthm1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmthm1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmthm1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Non-Vanishing Updates in Sparse-Reward Regimes)<span id="Thmthm1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmthm1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmthm1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Define the shaped surrogate <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{{shaped}}(\theta)\doteq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≐</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{{shaped}}(\theta)\doteq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, and the PPO surrogate <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{{ppo}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,A_{t}\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{{ppo}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,A_{t}\right].</annotation></semantics></math> Consider a training iteration <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> such that the expected magnitude of the PPO
advantage is small, i.e., <math id="Thmthm1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[|A_{t}|]\leq\varepsilon_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[|A_{t}|]\leq\varepsilon_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> for some
<math id="Thmthm1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{A}\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{A}\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>–<a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the expected norm of the
shaped PPO policy update satisfies</span></p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigl\|\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{shaped}}\bigr\|\;\geq\;\xi_{k}\,\bigl\|\mathcal{L}_{k}^{U}\bigr\|-O(\varepsilon_{A})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>shaped</mi></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.280em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≥</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>U</mi></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigl\|\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\mathrm{shaped}}\bigr\|\;\geq\;\xi_{k}\,\bigl\|\mathcal{L}_{k}^{U}\bigr\|-O(\varepsilon_{A}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmthm1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where
<math id="Thmthm1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{k}^{U}\doteq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,U_{t}\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>U</mi></msubsup><mo>≐</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{k}^{U}\doteq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,U_{t}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Proof.</span> Deferred to Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:38%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/new_envs.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:209/142;" width="209" height="142" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Evaluation environments. Top: <span id="S3.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span> (navigation to target), <span id="S3.F3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LavaCrossing</span> (long-horizon navigation with irreversible hazards), <span id="S3.F3.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> (sparse reward with key–goal dependency).

<br class="ltx_break">Bottom: <span id="S3.F3.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span> (sequence-sensitive toggling), <span id="S3.F3.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span> (distractor-rich variant with key-goal dependency).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We validate our method through extensive experiments implemented using the RLlib <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Our evaluation focuses on performance gains, sample efficiency, and the computational overhead introduced by LLM integration.
The objective is to characterize the benefits and trade-offs of incorporating LLM guidance in RL, including how different levels of LLM capabilities influence the policy learning dynamics and final policy quality.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Simulation Platform</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider six distinct environments, which are selected to span discrete vs. visual inputs, short- vs. long-horizon dependencies, reversible vs. irreversible dynamics, and with vs. without perceptual distractors, forming a compact yet representative benchmark for sparse-reward RL.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Gymnasium ToyText.</span> Gymnasium <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arnoldo and others, 2024</a>)</cite> provides simple tabular environments for controlled analysis of learning dynamics in low-dimensional settings. Despite their simplicity, these environments feature sparse rewards and require strategic exploration, making them suitable for isolating the early-stage benefits of memory-guided utility shaping. We include <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span> as a minimal benchmark where PPO reliably converges to the optimal policy, enabling us to verify that MIRA preserves convergence while accelerating early learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MiniGrid and BabyAI.</span> MiniGrid <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and BabyAI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019</a>)</cite> are suites of lightweight, procedurally generated environments designed to evaluate exploration and planning in partially observable, sparse-reward settings.
We use these tasks to assess the effectiveness of advantage shaping in long-horizon decision-making environments that require reasoning under uncertainty and robustness to irrelevant stimuli. We include five tasks, selected to cover diverse challenges involving planning, credit assignment, and distraction resilience (Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
We use pixel-based observations (RGB images) rendered from the environment as the policy inputs, to introduce perceptual complexity and evaluate agent performance under a more realistic observation setting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Baseline Methods</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">PPO (RL baseline). </span> We train a tabula rasa PPO agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017a</a>)</cite> that learns purely from environment interaction and rewards. Network architecture, PPO hyperparameters, and rollout settings are held fixed across all methods for fair comparison.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Hierarchical RL. </span> We include hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Matthews et al., 2022</a>)</cite> as a baseline that uses pre-trained LLM option policies for temporal abstraction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM-RS. </span> We consider the method of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhambri et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which we refer to as LLM-RS. This approach queries the LLM in real time to generate plans for potential-based reward shaping, with a verifier refining them for valid action sequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LLM4Teach. </span> We include LLM4Teach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as a representative teacher-based approach. It employs a pre-trained LLM as a policy teacher and guides the RL agent through policy distillation, and is among the state-of-the-art methods in this category.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To assess how effectively MIRA addresses the challenges raised in the introduction, we structure our core experiments around three guiding questions. These questions examine whether utility-shaped advantages compensate for PPO’s weak early gradients in sparse-reward, long-horizon, and partially observable settings, and whether amortizing limited LLM guidance into a persistent memory structure provides sufficient return while supporting scalability and avoiding latency. Formally:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q1</span><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How does MIRA improve early learning efficiency and convergence relative to PPO, even when PPO’s final performance is competitive?</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q2</span><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How well does MIRA perform in long-horizon environments that demand extended exploration and multi-step reasoning?</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q3</span><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How effectively does MIRA translate a limited number of LLM queries into performance gains compared to query-heavy methods?</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">To isolate the contribution of individual components in MIRA’s design, we further conduct ablations organized around three additional questions. These probe how online queries complement offline-initialized memory, and how sensitive MIRA is to degraded, incorrect, or stylistically varied LLM outputs. Formally:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q4</span><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How do online LLM queries improve learning, beyond what offline memory provides?</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q5</span><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How does MIRA handle late-stage exposure to degraded LLM guidance once its memory is well-formed?</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Q6</span><span id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">: How do variations in LLM reasoning affect memory and downstream results?</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> provides additional results, including evaluations on unseen seeds to assess generalization, <span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">wall-clock analyses of LLM-query overhead (Figure <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Relative Wall Time ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>), and measurements of memory growth (Figure <a href="#A7.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ G.4 Memory Growth Analysis ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>). We also report ablations on the screening threshold (Figure <a href="#A7.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ G.1.2 Threshold Sensitivity ‣ G.1 Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>) and prompt wording (Figure <a href="#A7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>), each examining its effect on overall learning behavior and addressing aspects of Q5.</span> In addition, supplementary plots from sweeps over shaping weights (Figure <a href="#A7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ G.2 Early Advantage Dynamics ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>) are included to analyze their impact on early-stage learning dynamics and reward progression.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q1:</span> We evaluate <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">two variants of MIRA on <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake-8x8</span>, an offline-only version and an online-only version,</span> and compare them to the PPO baseline, averaging results over four seeds.
In the offline variant, three zero-shot GPT-o4-mini queries generate an initial memory graph. The LLM observes the grid layout (matching the agent’s full observability) but does not receive the slipperiness probability, which is hidden from both.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, this initialization results in faster early learning, and the offline variant maintains a higher return than PPO throughout, and the online-only variant in the first 1K iterations. The online-only variant begins with an empty memory graph, without any global information about the map and issues LLM queries during training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/new_froznelake.jpg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:274/125;" width="274" height="125" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Mean return on <span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span> (left): <span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Both MIRA variants improve early-stage learning relative to PPO, while PPO eventually attains a comparable asymptotic return.</span> Evolution of shaping terms <math id="S4.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.F4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and ratio <math id="S4.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (right): <math id="S4.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> decays during training, ensuring convergence as <math id="S4.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">S<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">ince the layout is deterministic and the action set is small, these online queries can infer short segments from the agent’s rollouts and populate the memory graph as training progresses.</span>
This provides a faster improvement rate than the offline variant, though it requires more LLM queries.
PPO eventually catches up, and by convergence, the asymptotic returns of all three methods become comparable.
During training, the shaping signal primarily affects the early iterations. As the policy improves, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> increases, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> decreases, <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">i.e. the shaping ratio <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}=\xi_{t}/\eta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">δ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ξ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">/</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">η</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}=\xi_{t}/\eta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> decays, reducing reliance on memory.</span> Under standard stochastic approximation conditions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kushner and Yin, 2003</a>)</cite>, this decay keeps the critic error within an <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(\delta_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(\delta_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> neighborhood of the true value, which vanishes as <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{t}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{t}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q2:</span> We next evaluate MIRA on five tasks designed to isolate distinct challenges in sparse and partially observable environments.
Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows mean return and success rate across the four tasks, with performance averaged over four different seeds.
In simpler tasks such as <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span>, PPO shows moderate early gains but plateaus well below optimal performance. Although hierarchical RL eventually catches up, MIRA reaches optimal returns in under half the training iterations. In <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LavaCrossing</span>, PPO fails to improve beyond near-zero success, indicating ineffective exploration. Hierarchical RL improves steadily but converges more slowly than MIRA. In more complex tasks such as <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> and <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span>, MIRA achieves substantially higher success rates, approximately twice those of HRL, while also converging faster.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/new_all.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/202;" width="548" height="202" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Mean return (top) and success rate (bottom) across four MiniGrid and BabyAI tasks. MIRA consistently outperforms both baselines, achieving faster learning, higher asymptotic return, and greater success rates. These results are obtained with a small LLM budget, using fewer than ten offline prompts to build memory graphs plus infrequent online queries to guide exploration.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These gains are achieved with a limited LLM query budget that combines offline and infrequent online access. Offline queries scale with task complexity. In <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span>, four zero-shot prompts to GPT-o4-mini are sufficient to build a useful memory graph, while <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> requires about seven queries that mix few-shot and zero-shot prompts.
Online queries are budgeted separately and also vary with task complexity. In <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span>, about seven online queries suffice to suppress irrelevant actions throughout training. In <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span>, queries are triggered more frequently early in training to help interpret partial observations and suggest short sequences, such as turning, that align the agent with the door. Once the red door is discovered and toggled, the offline memory becomes sufficient. In this task, rooms behind the doors serve only as distractors; baseline agents, including hierarchical RL, often waste steps exploring them. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (lower right), HRL achieves higher success rates than PPO but yields similar average return in the beginning due to suboptimal trajectory use. By contrast, MIRA avoids such inefficiencies by focusing on goal-relevant behavior earlier in training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/radar.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:220/135;" width="220" height="135" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Mean return (left): LLM4Teach shows faster early gains, while MIRA steadily improves and matches its final return with fewer queries. LLM-RS benefits early from reward shaping but plateaus lower.
Return per LLM query (right): Under two query budgets, MIRA achieves higher efficiency.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q3:</span> To further evaluate MIRA, we compare it to LLM4Teach and LLM-RS in the custom variant environment <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span>.
We also include a Sole LLM baseline, where GPT-o4-mini executes plans under full observability without learning.
Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows mean return progression at selected training checkpoints. For Sole LLM, we report average return over 100 seeds to demonstrate that the task is LLM-solvable and that its outputs provide useful structural guidance. The accompanying bar chart reports amortized return per cumulative LLM query under two fixed budgets <span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">(10 and 20 queries, both below the usage of any method)</span>, quantifying how each method translates queries into performance gains.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">MIRA achieves higher query efficiency than both LLM4Teach and LLM-RS, <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">using about <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">30</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30</annotation></semantics></math> queries per run</span> (seven offline and <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\pm 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\pm 3</annotation></semantics></math> online) to obtain higher return per query.
In contrast, LLM4Teach issues dense supervision, querying the LLM <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">once</span> on every state–action–reward triplet within training batches, <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">which in our experimental setup corresponds to more than <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">500</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500</annotation></semantics></math> queries</span> before the policy stabilizes.
LLM-RS, which uses LLM-generated reward code, queries once per layout, totaling over <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> calls in our setup. While lighter than LLM4Teach, this still requires layout-level access throughout training. Despite its heavier budget, LLM4Teach achieves comparable final performance to MIRA, while LLM-RS fails to match MIRA’s return. Notably, LLM-RS outpaces MIRA early due to reward shaping, but falls behind later.
LLM4Teach shows an early advantage through front-loaded queries, but at a significantly higher cost. Tables in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> report results on unseen evaluation seeds to assess generalization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Ablation Studies</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q4 </span><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">(Online Query Frequency)</span><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">:</span> 
We vary the number of online LLM queries issued during training of <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>, to assess how constrained usage affects learning efficiency and final performance. Each agent begins with the same memory graph, initialized from identical offline queries, isolating the contribution of dynamic LLM input from that of static memory initialization. We compare MIRA under three online budgets: zero, a mid budget of 10 queries, and a high budget of 20. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> (left), more frequent online access accelerates learning, with the large-budget variant achieving optimal return in fewer steps (Table <a href="#A7.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ G.5 Query Frequency Performance Summary ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a></span>). Even with just 10 online calls, MIRA substantially outperforms the offline-only variant. Nevertheless, MIRA (offline) still yields a notable boost over baseline PPO, indicating that static memory alone can provide meaningful guidance when dynamic access is unavailable.
<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Given this noticeable improvement over PPO, the offline-only variant is a practical choice when run-time LLM access is restricted or when latency makes online queries impractical, since it relies entirely on the memory graph constructed offline. When limited run-time access is available, the online variant becomes preferable because dynamic queries update the memory during exploration and accelerate learning, at the cost of additional wall-clock time associated with LLM calls (Figure <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Relative Wall Time ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>, Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>).</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/all_ab.png" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/97;" width="548" height="97" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="S4.F7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation Studies</span>.
Query frequency (left): Agents share the same offline memory but vary in online budgets. More queries accelerate learning, with high-budget agents achieving optimal returns more quickly.
Unreliable LLM (middle): With identical offline memory, screening is disabled and queries are swapped from GPT-o4-mini to Gemini Pro only in the late phase. Performance remains stable in the late phase, indicating reduced dependence on online guidance once policy have matured.
LLM models (right): Agents differ only in the LLM used for memory. Performance differences reflect divergent reasoning styles: Gemma3 induces inefficient checking, Claude favors cautious exploration, while Gemini Pro and o4-mini enable faster learning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q5 </span><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">(Unreliable LLM Outputs)</span><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">:</span> 
We evaluate a scenario where the LLM is swapped at a later training stage and the screening unit is disabled only for this final online phase in <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span> environment. All agents share the same offline-initialized memory graph and use GPT-o4-mini with screening during earlier online queries. In the final stage, we replace the LLM with Gemini Pro and omit screening. By this point, MIRA has accumulated sufficient experience and memory, allowing it to tolerate low-confidence or incorrect suggestions without collapsing performance. We prompted both LLMs with a scenario where the agent has already explored <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">thoroughly</span> and confirmed no key is present (implying it was already collected, since inventory is <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unobserved</span>).
When asked which action to down-weight, GPT-o4-mini gave a consistent suppression, whereas Gemini returned a misaligned alternative. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> (middle), MIRA remains stable under degraded guidance, though convergence slows and final return drops slightly. Details of the LLM responses are shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ D.4 Case Study: Distracted DoorKey ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Q6 </span><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">(Reasoning and Performance)</span><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">:</span>
We assess MIRA’s sensitivity to the choice of language model by replacing GPT-o4-mini with alternatives such as GPT-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite>, Claude Sonnet 4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemma 3 27B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ananthanarayanan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. All models go through the same process to ensure comparability. Unlike the ablation done before, the model swap is applied from the beginning of training.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> (right), the reasoning style shaping the memory graph strongly impacts downstream RL performance.
For instance, Gemma3 performs poorly because it recommends checking the door after every pickup, leading to wasteful steps.
Claude adopts an exploratory policy that yields slow but eventual progress, showing early improvement followed by plateauing, but it eventually recovers as the memory is dynamic.
GeminiPro and GPT-o4-mini both enable fast early learning, but o4-mini’s memory includes <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">detours</span> that prove beneficial later, ultimately reaching the highest asymptotic return.
These differences highlight how the reasoning processes behind LLM outputs directly influence MIRA’s long-term policy quality. Figure <a href="#A4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ D.3 LLM Reasoning Patterns Across Models ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a></span> presents the reasoning traces produced by different LLM models used.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose MIRA, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that integrates large language model (LLM) guidance via a memory graph built from high-return trajectories and LLM-inferred information. By shaping advantage estimates with a utility signal derived from this memory, MIRA accelerates early learning without requiring continuous LLM supervision. Theoretical and empirical results on sparse-reward tasks confirm improved sample efficiency and preserved convergence. Limitations of the current design are discussed in Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Limitations ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>.
<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Extending MIRA to continuous-control and vision-based domains is a natural next step. Prior LLM-guided robotics work shows that semantic subgoals can be grounded in continuous spaces through learned affordances or visual embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. In such settings, MIRA’s discrete similarity function can be replaced with comparisons in a latent representation space, e.g., using encoder features or R3M-style embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nair et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, while memory scalability can be maintained through clustered or hierarchical organization. These adaptations would allow MIRA’s memory graph and utility-based shaping to apply beyond grid worlds and support longer-horizon tasks with richer state spaces.</span> Extending MIRA to multi-goal domains such as Crafter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, where reusable subgoal structure is prominent, is another promising direction.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have taken several steps to ensure reproducibility of our results.
All theoretical assumptions and complete proofs are included in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> details the environment specifications and the exact LLM prompts used for both offline and online queries.
Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Reproducibility ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> lists the full set of hyperparameters for MIRA across every evaluated environment.
We also provide pseudocodes for all proposed algorithms in Algorithms <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.4 Adaptive Advantage Shaping ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> through  <a href="#alg5" title="Algorithm 5 ‣ F.2 Goal Alignment ‣ Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, ensuring clarity and transparency despite their straightforward implementation. The code is available at paper’s webpage <a href="https://narjesno.github.io/MIRA/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://narjesno.github.io/MIRA/</a>.
Together, these materials supply all information necessary to reproduce our experiments and verify the claims of the paper.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Appendix</h2>

<div id="Ax1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The supplemental material is organized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="Ax1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="Ax1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="Ax1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Ax1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Ax1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Section <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Background ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a></span> reviews <span id="Ax1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">background</span> on reinforcement learning definitions and policy gradient algorithms to make the paper self-contained.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Ax1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Ax1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Ax1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Section <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Related Works ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a></span> discusses <span id="Ax1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">related work</span> relevant to our approach in more depth.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Ax1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Ax1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Ax1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Section <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a></span> presents the <span id="Ax1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">theoretical</span> results and supporting proofs for our method.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Ax1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="Ax1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Ax1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Section <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a></span> describes the <span id="Ax1.I1.i4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LLM prompting procedures</span> in MIRA and presents the corresponding <span id="Ax1.I1.i4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reasoning</span> traces.</p>
