<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Background</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Standard Reinforcement Learning</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement learning (RL) is typically modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP), defined by a tuple <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is the state space, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> the action space, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> the transition function, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> the reward function, and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma\in[0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma\in[0,1)</annotation></semantics></math> the discount factor.
The agent’s behavior is determined by a policy <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, which defines a probability distribution over actions given the current state: <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>. Learning proceeds through interaction with the environment, producing trajectories, sequences of states, actions, and rewards of the form <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},r_{0},s_{1},a_{1},r_{1},\dots)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},r_{0},s_{1},a_{1},r_{1},\dots)</annotation></semantics></math>, and using them to improve the policy.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The objective is to learn a policy that maximizes the expected return, defined as the discounted sum of rewards along a trajectory:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The environment’s reward function implicitly defines the final goal (<math id="A1.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}</annotation></semantics></math>) by assigning reward to behaviors that accomplish the task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al., 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silver, 2015</a>)</cite>.
To estimate this objective, RL algorithms often make use of value functions, which quantify the long-term utility of states or state-action pairs. The state-value function <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the expected return when starting from state <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> and following policy <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The action-value function <math id="A1.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> further conditions on the first action taken and is defined as:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="Q(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.1 </span>Partial Observability and Credit Assignment Challenges</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In many real-world scenarios, the environment is only partially observable. In such cases, the MDP generalizes to a partially observable MDP (POMDP), defined by the tuple <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma,\mathcal{O},\Omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>γ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma,\mathcal{O},\Omega)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math> is the observation space and <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega</annotation></semantics></math> is the observation function. The agent does not directly observe the true state <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math>; instead, it receives observations <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from an observation space <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}</annotation></semantics></math>, sampled via <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(o_{t}|s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(o_{t}|s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, and must rely on its history of observations and actions to make decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib98" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaelbling et al., 1998</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These difficulties are further amplified in environments where the agents face sparse and delayed rewards. Sparse rewards refer to the limited presence of nonzero rewards since this feedback is only provided upon reaching specific goals (i.e., <math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(s_{t},a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(s_{t},a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> is typically zero until the agent reaches the final goal state (<math id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}</annotation></semantics></math>) defined by the task). On the other hand, delayed rewards refer to settings where the consequences of an action are not reflected in the reward until several steps later. In both cases, the agent must reason over long horizons to determine which actions contributed to the eventual outcome, a challenge known as the credit assignment problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2015a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Credit assignment is closely tied to the broader challenge of exploration. Inefficient exploration occurs when the agent fails to sufficiently cover the state space, limiting its ability to discover high-return trajectories and improve its policy.
This problem is exacerbated in high-dimensional environments, where the number of possible state-action sequences grows exponentially and random exploration becomes increasingly unlikely to encounter informative transitions with sparse or delayed rewards. In such cases, the combination of large search spaces and limited reward signals often leads to slow convergence, poor sample efficiency, and high variance in learning outcomes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.1.2 </span>Subgoals and Abstractions</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In long-horizon tasks, reinforcement learning agents often benefit from structuring behavior around subgoals, intermediate objectives that facilitate progress toward the overall task. The concept of subgoals in reinforcement learning originated in hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL), where it was formalized through the use of temporally extended actions.
In particular, the options framework introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutton et al. (1999)</a></cite> defines options as high-level actions composed of an initiation set, a policy, and a termination condition, often interpreted as achieving a subgoal <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stolle and Precup, 2002</a>)</cite>.
These subgoals correspond to intermediate states or conditions that decompose long-horizon tasks into smaller, temporally coherent segments that make the final goal more attainable when reached.
More broadly, subgoals provide structure for reasoning over extended time horizons and facilitate learning in sparse-reward settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While early approaches focused on explicit or learned state-based subgoals, recent work has explored abstract subgoals that capture semantic or latent-level progress. These abstractions may not correspond to a specific state but instead reflect high-level intentions and meaningful progress (e.g., opening a door, entering a room, or collecting an object).
Such abstractions enable reasoning at a higher level of granularity and are especially useful in environments with sparse rewards or delayed feedback. Subgoal discovery and abstraction have also been explored in curriculum learning, imitation learning, and human-in-the-loop frameworks to improve exploration and sample efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">MacGlashan et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shiarlis et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Narvekar et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Policy Gradient Methods</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Policy gradient methods directly optimize a parameterized policy <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> by ascending the gradient of expected return. The objective is to find parameters <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> that maximize:</p>
<table id="A1.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></munderover><mrow><msup><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a trajectory generated by following the current policy.
The gradient of this objective can be estimated via the likelihood ratio trick, yielding the REINFORCE estimator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams, 1992</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="A1.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})R\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})R\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the return from time <math id="A1.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> onward. While theoretically sound and unbiased, this estimator suffers from high variance, making it challenging to apply in practice without further refinement.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">A.2.1 </span>Advantage-Based Policy Optimization</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To reduce variance and improve sample efficiency, modern policy gradient algorithms often use advantage functions, which quantify the relative quality of an action compared to the policy’s baseline behavior. The advantage function is defined as:</p>
<table id="A1.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> is the expected return from taking action <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> in state <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is the expected return from <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> under policy <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.
Using this formulation, the policy gradient becomes:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})A\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})A\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">which improves stability while preserving unbiasedness.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This idea underpins a family of actor-critic algorithms, where the actor updates the policy using the advantage-weighted gradient, and the critic estimates value functions used to compute <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. Representative algorithms in this class include A2C and A3C <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mnih et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, which leverage parallel actors to accelerate training and stabilize updates, and PPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017b</a>)</cite>, which constrains policy updates by clipping the policy ratio in the surrogate objective:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{\text{PPO}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\left[\min(r_{t}A_{t},\text{clip}(r_{t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{t})\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>PPO</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>clip</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{\text{PPO}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\left[\min(r_{t}A_{t},\text{clip}(r_{t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{t})\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> is a small trust region parameter that limits how much the policy is allowed to change at each update.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">These methods are widely used in modern deep reinforcement learning due to their scalability and consistent empirical performance across a range of tasks. Since MIRA operates by shaping the advantage function, it is compatible with any policy optimization method that relies on advantage-weighted updates.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Language Model Guidance in RL </h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A growing line of work explores how large language models (LLMs) can be integrated into reinforcement learning by framing them as auxiliary components within the agent–environment loop.
A recent taxonomy by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al. (2024)</a></cite> outlines the roles of LLMs in RL along four key dimensions: information processors, reward designers, decision-makers, and generators.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As <span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">information processors</span>, LLMs extract and organize task-relevant knowledge from natural language, environment descriptions, or prior experience. This includes synthesizing high-level goals, parsing instructions, and transforming language input into actionable constraints or representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shinn and others, 2023</a>)</cite>. A common approach is to use frozen pre-trained models to encode task-relevant features without fine-tuning, though they may perform poorly on out-of-distribution data due to limited adaptability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paischer et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paischer et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.

<br class="ltx_break">Alternatively, fine-tuned models can better align with task-specific distributions, leading to more robust RL performance and improved generalization in unseen environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Poudel et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. In addition, LLMs can convert human instructions or task prompts into formal representations or structured goals, and interpret descriptions of the environment, such as objects, layouts, or dynamics, into usable priors for downstream RL modules. This reduces the burden of language comprehension for RL agents and improves sample efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Basavatia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sumers et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
These models can decouple information processing from control, with the LLM handling language grounding and feature extraction while the policy module focuses on decision-making. Such capabilities can reduce learning complexity and accelerate policy acquisition by shaping the agent’s representation space early in training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As <span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reward designers</span>, LLMs provide auxiliary supervision by scoring agent behavior or generating rewards.
This can take the form of natural language critiques, programmatic reward code, or goal-conditioned evaluations. In the implicit reward setting, LLMs serve as proxy reward models by either being directly prompted to evaluate agent behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or by computing alignment between visual observations and language goals using pretrained vision-language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adeniji et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seo et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grauman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. These methods enable reward shaping via natural language instructions or preference feedback and have been shown to improve learning efficiency and generalization. In the explicit reward setting, LLMs are used to generate executable code that defines reward functions programmatically. This includes frameworks that iteratively refine reward code using self-reflection and feedback from training outcomes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madaan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>. Compared to manually engineered rewards, these LLM-generated functions offer transparency and adaptability, and in some cases match or exceed human performance, especially in complex manipulation tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As <span id="A2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">decision-makers</span>, LLMs output action plans, policy sketches, or even direct action sequences based on current observations.
These methods embed LLMs tightly into the decision loop, either guiding exploration or dictating behavior in few-shot or zero-shot settings. One approach leverages pre-trained LLMs for direct action generation, often adapting transformer-based models like Decision Transformers to treat offline RL as a sequence modeling problem. These LLM-backed policies show improved generalization, particularly in sparse-reward and long-horizon tasks, by transferring latent structure learned from large-scale language data. Some methods further fine-tune LLMs using task-specific trajectories or append small task-specific modules to facilitate adaptation, achieving notable gains in sample efficiency and task transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mezghani et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.

<br class="ltx_break">Other works integrate LLMs more loosely as action guides, generating action candidates or expert priors to support exploration and training. For example, LLMs can prune the action space by proposing high-probability candidates or decompose complex goals into sequential subtasks, improving exploration in environments with large or unstructured action spaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hausknecht et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dalal et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. They have also been used to regularize policy updates, align agent behavior with human intent, or inject expert-level motion plans. Across both low-level and strategic roles, LLM-based decision-making enables agents to learn from rich, structured priors and execute more informed behaviors in complex settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As <span id="A2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">generators</span>, LLMs contribute to reinforcement learning by either simulating environmental dynamics or providing policy-level explanations to enhance transparency. In the simulation role, LLMs function as world model simulators that generate trajectories or learn latent dynamics representations from multimodal data, thereby improving sample efficiency in model-based RL. Recent work has leveraged Transformer-based architectures to model complex visual or sequential environments, demonstrating gains in generalization and long-horizon reasoning. These models either auto-regressively generate rollouts from pre-trained dynamics or use representation learning to predict future states and rewards, often incorporating language as an additional modality for grounding and abstraction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Micheli et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robine et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Separately, LLMs have been used as policy interpreters to generate human-readable explanations of agent behavior from state-action histories or decision trees. This facilitates interpretability, improves human trust, and can inform reward design or debugging, though current work has focused mainly on policy-level summaries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">While MIRA incorporates elements of information processing and LLMs as generators, its overall orientation remains distinct and more RL-centric from prior LLM-centered approaches. Rather than positioning the LLM as a decision-maker or continuous feedback provider, MIRA relegates it to a supporting role that gradually fades over time. LLM outputs are used intermittently to enrich a structured memory graph that informs, but does not dictate, learning. The primary learning signal remains grounded in environment interaction, with utility shaping softly modulating advantage estimates rather than overriding the reward function. This design prioritizes policy optimization through reinforcement learning rather than imitation or prompting</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Memory and Buffers in RL</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Augmenting RL agents with structured memory has been proposed as a means of supporting generalization, planning, and long-horizon credit assignment.
Early works such as Neural Episodic Control (NEC) and other episodic value-based methods enabled agents to recall high-value past experiences for more sample-efficient decision-making via memory buffers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pritzel et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blundell et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin, 1992</a>)</cite>.
Subsequent approaches extended this idea by integrating differentiable memory into policy networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Other methods introduce structured representations, such as subgoal graphs or navigation maps, to facilitate hierarchical planning, exploration, or navigation in partially observable environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beeching et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rana et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Across these directions, the common pattern is to directly query stored structures, either through replay, imitation, or graph traversal, to guide behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MIRA aligns with this direction by maintaining a structured memory graph populated with high-return trajectory segments but departs from this pattern in several key ways.
First, its memory graph is co-constructed from high-return agent trajectories and LLM-inferred subgoals, enabling abstraction and structure difficult to obtain early through interaction alone.
Second, rather than querying memory for action selection or value estimation, MIRA distills the stored information into a utility signal that modulates advantage estimates during training.
This indirect shaping avoids disrupting the optimization loop or overfitting to specific stored transitions.
Finally, MIRA maintains a compact memory via pruning and infrequent updates, which avoids the inefficiencies of excessive memory or the brittleness of sparse guidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib86" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Zou, 2018</a>)</cite>.
This makes MIRA more scalable and better suited for tasks where long-term structure must complement autonomous learning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Advantage Modifications in RL</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modifying the advantage function has been studied as a way to stabilize learning and improve sample efficiency in policy optimization. A common approach adjusts the estimation process to better balance bias and variance. Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2015b</a>)</cite> introduces a tunable parameter that interpolates between high-bias low-variance and low-bias high-variance estimators, and is widely adopted in actor-critic algorithms. Other methods reformulate policy updates in terms of advantages. Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2019</a>)</cite> avoids policy gradients and instead performs weighted regression over actions. P3O <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fakoor et al., 2020</a>)</cite> combines on-policy and off-policy learning by applying advantage-weighted importance sampling to stabilize updates.
In the offline RL setting, advantage estimates are often used to filter experience and address distributional shift. Advantage-based data selection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib94" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kostrikov et al., 2021</a>)</cite> discards transitions with low advantage, helping to focus learning on high-quality samples. Additional work incorporates auxiliary signals into the advantage estimate. Preference-based RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2021</a>)</cite> derives implicit advantage signals from human comparisons, while other approaches integrate value correction from ensemble critics or confidence measures to adjust learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MIRA builds on these ideas but takes a different path. Instead of replacing the estimator or introducing new objectives, it shapes the advantage using a utility term derived from a structured memory graph. This utility reflects agent experience and LLM-derived subgoals, allowing guidance without overriding reward feedback. The resulting signal is integrated into PPO’s update rule without disrupting its optimization dynamics, enabling structured shaping while maintaining scalability and convergence guarantees.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">

<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since the utility term does not alter the policy or critic structure, and enters additively, MIRA preserves standard stability and asymptotic properties of policy gradient methods such as PPO under standard assumptions:</p>
</div>

<div id="Thmass3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_ass">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmass3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 3</span></span><span id="Thmass3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Trust region)<span id="Thmass3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmass3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{KL}\!\left(\pi_{k},\pi_{k+1}\right)\leq\frac{(1-\gamma)\,\varepsilon_{k}^{2}}{2}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mpadded style="width:0.511em;" width="0.511em"><mi>L</mi></mpadded><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{KL}\!\left(\pi_{k},\pi_{k+1}\right)\leq\frac{(1-\gamma)\,\varepsilon_{k}^{2}}{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmass3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmass3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(implied by PPO clip ratio <math id="Thmass3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\pi}\in[1-\varepsilon_{k},1+\varepsilon_{k}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\pi}\in[1-\varepsilon_{k},1+\varepsilon_{k}]</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Stability and Safety Results</h3>

<div id="Thmlem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 1</span></span><span id="Thmlem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Bounded Shaped Policy Updates)<span id="Thmlem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (Boundedness), <a href="#Thmass2" title="Assumption 2 (Scale control). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (Scale Control), and
<a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (Trust Region), the magnitude of each shaped PPO policy update is uniformly bounded.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">By definition, the shaped advantage satisfies</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\tilde{A}_{t}|\leq\eta_{t}|A_{t}|+\xi_{t}|U_{t}|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\tilde{A}_{t}|\leq\eta_{t}|A_{t}|+\xi_{t}|U_{t}|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text">Using Assumption <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Assumption <a href="#Thmass2" title="Assumption 2 (Scale control). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a), we obtain</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\tilde{A}_{t}|\leq\eta_{t}A_{\max}+\xi_{t}U_{\max}\leq\eta_{t}A_{\max}+\delta_{t}\eta_{t}U_{\max}\leq(1+\delta_{t})A_{\max}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\tilde{A}_{t}|\leq\eta_{t}A_{\max}+\xi_{t}U_{\max}\leq\eta_{t}A_{\max}+\delta_{t}\eta_{t}U_{\max}\leq(1+\delta_{t})A_{\max}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Under the PPO trust-region constraint in Assumption <a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the likelihood ratio is clipped and
the score function <math id="A3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> has bounded second moment.
Consequently, the policy gradient update</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{k}^{{shaped}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{k}^{{shaped}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">is uniformly bounded in norm.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmthm2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmthm2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span id="Thmthm2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Non-Divergence under Trust Region)<span id="Thmthm2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmthm2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmthm2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (Boundedness),
<a href="#Thmass2" title="Assumption 2 (Scale control). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (Scale Control), and
<a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (Trust Region),
the PPO updates computed using the shaped advantage
<math id="Thmthm2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>
remain within the prescribed trust region.
In particular, the KL divergence between successive policies
is uniformly bounded, and the optimization does not diverge.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">At iteration <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, PPO computes the policy update by maximizing a clipped surrogate
objective of the form</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{k}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\!\big(r_{t}(\theta)\,\tilde{A}_{t},\;\operatorname{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{k},1+\varepsilon_{k})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\big)\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.497em;" width="0.497em"><mi>𝔼</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.653em;" width="1.653em"><mi>min</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>clip</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{k}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\!\big(r_{t}(\theta)\,\tilde{A}_{t},\;\operatorname{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{k},1+\varepsilon_{k})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\big)\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text">where <math id="A3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{k}}(a_{t}|s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{k}}(a_{t}|s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The clipping operation enforces</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}(\theta)\in[1-\varepsilon_{k},\,1+\varepsilon_{k}]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn> 1</mn><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}(\theta)\in[1-\varepsilon_{k},\,1+\varepsilon_{k}],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text">which implies the trust-region bound in Assumption <a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>
(see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al. (2017b)</a></cite>).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">This constraint depends only on the policy parameterization and the clipping
threshold <math id="A3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>, and is independent of the specific form of the
advantage estimator.
Therefore, optimizing the shaped surrogate induces the same likelihood-ratio
constraint as standard PPO.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">By Lemma <a href="#Thmlem1" title="Lemma 1 (Bounded Shaped Policy Updates). ‣ C.2 Stability and Safety Results ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (Bounded Shaped Policy Updates), the resulting
policy update has uniformly bounded magnitude.
Combining bounded update magnitude with the likelihood-ratio constraint yields</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{k}\,\|\,\pi_{k+1})\leq\tfrac{(1-\gamma)\varepsilon_{k}^{2}}{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>ε</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{k}\,\|\,\pi_{k+1})\leq\tfrac{(1-\gamma)\varepsilon_{k}^{2}}{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p5.2.1" class="ltx_text">Hence, the sequence of shaped PPO updates remains within the prescribed trust
region, and the optimization does not diverge.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Asymptotic Behavior</h3>

<div id="Thmthm3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_thm">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmthm3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3</span></span><span id="Thmthm3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Asymptotic Equivalence to PPO)<span id="Thmthm3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmthm3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Thmthm3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmthm3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\pi_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\pi_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math> be the sequence of policies produced by PPO using the shaped advantage</span></p>
<table id="A3.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Thmthm3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmthm3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="Thmthm3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed on-policy from the same rollouts as <math id="Thmthm3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (Boundedness), <a href="#Thmass2" title="Assumption 2 (Scale control). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (Scale Control), and
<a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (Trust Region), the shaped update is asymptotically equivalent to the standard PPO update.
In particular, any stationary point of PPO is also a stationary point of the shaped objective.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">The PPO policy gradient update with shaped advantage is given by</span></p>
<table id="A3.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{{shaped}}_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{(s_{t},a_{t})\sim\pi_{k}}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\big]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{{shaped}}_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{(s_{t},a_{t})\sim\pi_{k}}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})\,\tilde{A}_{t}\big].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text">Substituting the definition of <math id="A3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> yields</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>

<table id="A3.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">
