</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">By Assumption <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, both <math id="A3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are uniformly bounded.
Under the trust-region constraint in Assumption <a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the score function
<math id="A3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> has bounded second moment, ensuring that
both gradient components are finite.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">By Assumption <a href="#Thmass2" title="Assumption 2 (Scale control). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b),</span></p>
<table id="A3.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{k\to\infty}\eta_{k}=1,\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\xi_{k}=0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.889em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{k\to\infty}\eta_{k}=1,\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\xi_{k}=0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text">which implies</span></p>
<table id="A3.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{L}_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\text{PPO}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>k</mi><mtext>PPO</mtext></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathcal{L}_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{k}^{\text{PPO}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">Therefore, the shaped update converges to the standard PPO update.
Any policy <math id="A3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying <math id="A3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{\text{PPO}}(\pi^{\star})=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>PPO</mtext></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{\text{PPO}}(\pi^{\star})=0</annotation></semantics></math> is also a stationary
point of the shaped objective asymptotically.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Early-Training Advantage</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem</span>[reinstate] (Non-Vanishing Updates in Sparse-Reward Regimes)<span id="A3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Recall that the shaped advantage is defined as</span></p>

<div id="A3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">By assumption, the expected magnitude of the PPO advantage is small,
<math id="A3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[|A_{t}|]\leq\varepsilon_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[|A_{t}|]\leq\varepsilon_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under Assumption <a href="#Thmass1" title="Assumption 1 (Boundedness). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <math id="A3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|A_{t}|\leq A_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|A_{t}|\leq A_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, and under the trust-region
constraint (Assumption <a href="#Thmass3" title="Assumption 3 (Trust region). ‣ C.1 Assumptions ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), the score function
<math id="A3.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> has bounded second moment.
Consequently, there exists a constant <math id="A3.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that</span></p>
<table id="A3.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<section id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Remark (Bias–Variance Trade-off).</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The shaping mechanism can also be interpreted through the lens of the
bias–variance trade-off in policy gradient estimation.
Standard PPO relies on advantage estimates (e.g., GAE or Monte Carlo returns)
that depend on long-horizon rollouts and typically exhibit high variance,
particularly in early training.
In contrast, the utility signal <math id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> depends only on the current state–action
pair and its similarity to stored high-return trajectories, yielding a
lower-variance but biased learning signal.
Initializing <math id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{0}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{0}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> stabilizes early optimization by injecting this bias,
while the decay schedule <math id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{k}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{k}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math> gradually restores reliance on
reward-based advantage estimates as the policy and critic become more reliable.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>LLM Prompting and Reasoning</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Gymnasium Toy text</h3>

<figure id="A4.F8" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:25%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/f8.png" id="A4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:124/124;" width="124" height="124" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Frozen Lake (Gymnasium)</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span> is a tabular RL environment where the agent starts in the top-left and must reach the bottom-right goal while avoiding holes.
For <span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span>, we provide the LLM with the complete map of the environment, either as an image (Figure <a href="#A4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ D.1 Gymnasium Toy text ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>) or as a serialized array representation such as <span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[‘F’, ‘F’, …, ‘H’, ‘F’, …, ‘G’]</span>. Though the environment is typically stochastic due to slipperiness, the LLM is instructed to assume deterministic transitions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A<span id="A4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">lthough much of the prompt is directly from the official environment description, for clarity and reproducibility, we include the full version.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/frozen_prompt.png" id="A4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/133;" width="548" height="133" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Prompt and response from GPT-4o-mini for the <span id="A4.F9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">FrozenLake</span> environment. The LLM receives a serialized map or a textual description and is asked to provide the best and second-best safe trajectories from start to goal, avoiding all holes under deterministic dynamics.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The prompt and the LLM’s response are shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ D.1 Gymnasium Toy text ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Standard and Custom MiniGrid and BabyAI Environments</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each environment was chosen for a specific purpose: <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span> involves short-horizon navigation and fast spatial goal acquisition. <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LavaCrossing</span> introduces irreversible transitions that require long-horizon planning to avoid dead ends. <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> requires the agent to acquire a key, unlock a door, and reach the goal, forming a delayed dependency chain that challenges temporal credit assignment.
<span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span> tests the agent’s ability to commit to a correct action sequence, as opening the blue door prematurely ends the episode. At last, <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span> introduces BabyAI-style distractors (e.g., irrelevant balls and boxes) alongside the original multi-step dependencies of <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>, allowing us to test whether the LLM can generalize across known task elements and maintain coherent subgoal proposals under added visual distraction.
For standard MiniGrid and BabyAI environments, we used the environment descriptions provided on the MiniGrid website. For our custom environment (<span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span>), we mimicked the phrasing and structure of the official MiniGrid descriptions (Figure <a href="#A4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ D.3 LLM Reasoning Patterns Across Models ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>). Unlike in <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Frozen Lake</span>, obtaining useful trajectories here was not as straightforward. MiniGrid-style environments often required multi-round prompting to obtain meaningful and desired outputs. Moreover, instead of providing an image of the environment, we found it more effective to use a textual description. This helped reduce confusion and encouraged the LLM to understand that object locations (e.g., the key, door, and agent in <span id="A4.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>) can vary across episodes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>LLM Reasoning Patterns Across Models</h3>

<figure id="A4.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/dd.png" id="A4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/86;" width="548" height="86" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Prompt to Offline LLM for the custom MiniGrid variant <span id="A4.F10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span>. The prompt describes the task setting, object roles, and challenges, and asks the LLM to confirm understanding before suggestions.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We observed that different LLMs produced very different memory graphs. To better understand how different models reason about these environments, we recorded
not only their output trajectories but also their internal reasoning processes. For model that include system-level thinking (e.g., GPT-o4-mini), this was extracted directly from the response. For models that do not expose intermediate reasoning (e.g., Claude 3), we followed up with an auxiliary prompt such as: “Give me your reasoning as to why you chose this sequence of actions.”</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/llms.png" id="A4.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:521/267;" width="521" height="267" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Reasoning traces produced by different LLMs in response to our custom environment prompt as part of “Offline LLM” prompting. After confirming they understood the environment, each model was asked: “If you were to give an RL agent useful trajectories to help solve this, what would you do?” For models that do not output internal reasoning (e.g., Claude), we issued a follow-up prompt requesting their thought process. We omit repeated environment restatements and show only the key parts where the model explains how it decided on the action sequence.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These responses were not used in the MIRA framework, but we found them surprisingly revealing. Despite receiving identical prompts, the models relied on starkly different reasoning strategies. This divergence gave us unexpected insight into how various LLMs process spatial structure, interpret decision sequences, and reason about reinforcement learning dynamics and learning objectives. Differences that, in turn, shape the quality of their output trajectories.
In Figure <a href="#A4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ D.3 LLM Reasoning Patterns Across Models ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, we present reasoning snippets from the LLMs’ outputs. We omit the initial sections where models repeat the prompt or restate the environment description, and instead highlight the specific reasoning steps that led each model to select a particular trajectory. The influence of these differing reasoning strategies on RL performance is reflected in the return curves shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Case Study: <span id="A4.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Distracted DoorKey</span></h3>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the ablation study presented in Subsections <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, GPT-o4-mini and Gemini return different outputs when presented with the same situation. Here, we provide the exact prompt and reasoning traces. As shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ D.4 Case Study: Distracted DoorKey ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, both responses appear plausible at a surface level, but only one is consistent with the task dynamics: given that sufficient exploration has already occurred, the key is likely collected, making suppression of the corresponding action the correct response. In this case, the divergence leads to a drop in performance under the misaligned output.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/gptgem.png" id="A4.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/140;" width="548" height="140" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Reasoning traces produced by Gemini and ChatGPT under “Online LLM” prompting. The prompt emphasizes that sufficient exploration has already been performed and, from the partial observation, no key is visible. A (flawed but plausible) line of reasoning is that the agent must still be in the phase of searching for the key, so reducing the probability of toggle appears reasonable to prioritize movement actions for exploration.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Memory Graph Construction Details</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we further explain the procedure for initializing, updating, and pruning MIRA’s memory graph. As discussed in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the initial memory graph is constructed from offline LLM-generated suggestions. Once built for a specific environment, this graph can be reused across training episodes or even across agents within the same task.
Since MIRA is designed to generalize across diverse settings, figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2.1 Memory Graph Design ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates how the framework accommodates environments with a single terminal objective as well as tasks with multiple independent objectives</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given that each task differs slightly, we largely focus our detailed explanation on <span id="A5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> from the MiniGrid suite for the rest of the subsections, as it contains multiple subgoals and is sufficiently complex to show the dynamics of the graph clearly.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Initialization</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in figure <a href="#A4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ D.3 LLM Reasoning Patterns Across Models ‣ Appendix D LLM Prompting and Reasoning ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, GPT-o4-mini tends to generate trajectory segments that begin after the key is picked up, with the subgoal “toggle the door”. In contrast, models like Claude tend to produce longer, full trajectories from the beginning.
Interestingly, segmented trajectories are often more useful in this environment.
Since the environment is partially observable and reinforcement learning relies heavily on exploration, allowing the agent to figure out how to reach the key on its own helps it understand the overall layout of the environment better.
Once the key is acquired, there is a higher chance that the door has already entered the agent’s observation window, making memory-guided navigation toward the door more effective.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to segments, the LLM also infers subgoals <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\kappa_{\ell})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\kappa_{\ell})</annotation></semantics></math>. While the obvious ones are “Pick up key,” “Open door,” and “Reach goal,” o4-mini returns more detailed versions like:</p>
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{1}:" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{1}:</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A5.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> Go to key → <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{2}:" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{2}:</annotation></semantics></math> Pick up key → <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{3}:" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{3}:</annotation></semantics></math> Go to door → <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{4}:" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>κ</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{4}:</annotation></semantics></math> Toggle door → <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}</annotation></semantics></math>: Go to goal</span>.</p>
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">This fine-grained subgoal sequence reflects the environment’s control logic: the “open door” action is valid only if the agent is positioned one step away, properly aligned, and facing the door.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, for each memory segment, an estimated subgoal reward <math id="A5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is stored in the node that reflects geometric progress toward completing its associated subgoal. In discrete environments (e.g., MiniGrid), progress is computed using the normalized shortest-path distance between the states in the segment and the subgoal’s target location.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Agent-Induced Updates</h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During training, new nodes are added to the memory graph or existing ones are updated whenever the agent produces trajectory segments that improve upon what the graph already stores, either by providing a new segment for a (sub)goal or by achieving a higher estimated return than the current entry for that (sub)goal. For example, if the agent independently discovers a shorter path to the key and then follows a memory-guided trajectory to reach the door or goal, the resulting sequence is added as a new node in the graph. Likewise, if the agent successfully executes a trajectory that was initially stored with low confidence from the offline LLM, we treat this behavior as implicit validation and increase the confidence of the corresponding memory node.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The memory graph remains lightweight throughout training. Each node stores a trajectory segment and metadata, and the total graph size stays compact. Compared to experience replay buffers in standard off-policy RL methods, which retain large volumes of data, the memory graph introduces negligible computational and memory overhead.
To maintain compactness, unused nodes are periodically pruned based on access frequency.
Each memory node tracks an access counter, which is reset every time the node is used. Nodes that are not accessed for 100 episodes are pruned, except for those corresponding to final goal trajectories (<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">g</mtext><mo>⊳</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textsl{g}_{\triangleright}</annotation></semantics></math>), which are retained since the agent might not have reached them early on, but they are essential for guiding successful completion later in training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ F.1 Similarity Score ‣ Appendix F Utility Computation ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the add, update, and prune operations that govern how the memory graph is maintained during training.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Online Grafting and Triggers</h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since the agent has a limited number of steps per episode, it may fail to reach any subgoal (e.g. “Open Door”) with a matching trajectory in the memory graph early on, preventing utility shaping from activating. To address this, MIRA includes a fallback mechanism: if the computed utility <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> is entirely zero for <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> consecutive episodes, the agent triggers an online LLM query. These online queries return short plans (e.g., “turn left, move forward, toggle”) based on the agent’s partial observations to help the agent reorient. Once screened for quality, the new suggestion is grafted into MIRA.
Another way online LLM queries contribute is by influencing the agent’s policy preferences directly through soft logit injection. Importantly, the online LLM is constrained by the same partial observability as the agent. It does not receive access to the full environment state and therefore cannot, for example, determine the presence of a key elsewhere in the grid. Furthermore, since inventory status is not part of the agent’s observation space, the LLM is unaware of whether the agent has picked up the key. Instead, the LLM receives a batch of recent partial observations and must infer from them whether any meaningful guidance can be offered.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Utility Computation</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the utility computation introduced in the main text, clarifying how each component contributes to the shaping term. The utility measures how closely the agent’s trajectory aligns with high-return segments stored in the memory graph. When a reference trajectory is matched, utility values are assigned based on reverse-aligned similarity with reference trajectories; unmatched steps receive zero utility. Below, we describe the role of each factor in the computation (Equation </span><a href="#S2.E2" title="In 2.3 Utility Signal Computation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="A6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">) and provide pseudocode for the full procedure.</span><span id="A6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">
</span></p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Similarity Score</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The similarity function assigns a score based on the information extracted from the agent’s and the reference transition’s observations. Depending on the environment, these observations may include position, orientation, or action. For example, in </span><span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FrozenLake</span><span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, observations are discrete and include only position, so direction is omitted in the similarity check. High similarity indicates that the agent is reproducing a locally meaningful portion of a successful stored trajectory, whereas low or zero similarity reflects small or no meaningful match. </span><span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<figure id="alg2" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 2</span> </span> Evolving Memory Graph During Training</figcaption>
<div id="alg2.6" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg2.l0" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">0:</span>
              
              
            <span id="alg2.l0.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> Memory graph </span><math id="alg2.l0.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#000000">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg2.l0.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">,

</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Goal Alignment</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The goal-alignment factor </span><math id="A6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> scales utility based on how closely the subgoal associated with a matched memory segment relates to the subgoal that the current transition corresponds to. Although the RL agent never observes subgoal labels, the </span><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">environment state</span><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> uniquely identifies which subgoal phase the transition belongs to, for example, in </span><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">DoorKey</span><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> environment, whether the agent is still approaching the key or has already picked it up and is proceeding toward the door.
Each memory node carries a subgoal label generated by the LLM. These subgoal descriptions consistently identify (i) the object or region involved and (ii) the high-level action applied to it. We extract these two components through simple rule-based parsing over the LLM-generated subgoals, yielding an entity token (e.g., key, door, ball) and an action-phase tag (e.g., navigate). The alignment score </span><math id="A6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> is then calculated as the Jaccard similarity between the token pair of the memory node’s subgoal and the token pair associated with the transition under evaluation.
As a result, locally similar transitions only contribute to utility when they align semantically with the relevant subgoal, preventing behaviorally similar but semantically unrelated memory segments from influencing the utility signal.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="alg4" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 4</span> </span> Goal Alignment <math id="alg4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math></figcaption>
<div id="alg4.6" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg4.l0" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">0:</span>
              
              
            <span id="alg4.l0.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> Agent </span><math id="alg4.l0.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ζ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta_{a}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l0.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and Reference </span><math id="alg4.l0.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ζ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta_{m}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l0.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> subgoal </span>
</div>
<div id="alg4.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
            <span id="alg4.l1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><math id="alg4.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{a}\leftarrow\textsc{tokens}(\zeta_{a})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_smallcaps" mathcolor="#000000">tokens</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ζ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">a</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{a}\leftarrow\textsc{tokens}(\zeta_{a})</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">  </span><math id="alg4.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="alg4.l1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">A</span><span id="alg4.l1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">gent entity–phase token </span>
</div>
<div id="alg4.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              
              
            <span id="alg4.l2.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><math id="alg4.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{m}\leftarrow\textsc{tokens}(\zeta_{m})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">t</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_smallcaps" mathcolor="#000000">tokens</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ζ</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi></msub><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{m}\leftarrow\textsc{tokens}(\zeta_{m})</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l2.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">  </span><math id="alg4.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math><span id="alg4.l2.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="alg4.l2.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">M</span><span id="alg4.l2.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">emory entity–phase token

<div id="A6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">With the similarity score </span><math id="A6.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathcolor="#000000">𝓈</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{s}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and alignment factor </span><math id="A6.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> established, we combine them with the memory-stored quantities </span><math id="A6.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">r</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">^</mo></mover><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (estimated subgoal reward) and </span><math id="A6.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">c</mi><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{m}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (LLM confidence) to construct the utility used in advantage shaping.</span><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>

<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Extended Experimental Studies</h2>

<figure id="A7.F13" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/twoprompt_v2.png" id="A7.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:242/120;" width="242" height="120" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span><span id="A7.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FrozenLake robustness to prompt wording. MIRA achieves similar performance under the original and alternative prompts, showing stability to natural variations in task description.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Sensitivity and Robustness Studies</h3>

<section id="A7.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">G.1.1 </span>Prompt Robustness</h4>

<div id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">T</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">o evaluate robustness to reasonable variations in prompt wording, we repeated the </span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FrozenLake</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> experiment using an alternative prompt with simpler phrasing but identical task information.</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">
</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">In this variant, the prompt stated that “</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FrozenLake is a grid where S is the start, G is the goal, F are safe tiles, and H are holes. The agent moves from state 0 using actions 0=left, 1=down, 2=right, 3=up, and moves that go off the grid keep the agent in place and are safe. Using the grid and assuming deterministic transitions, provide a shortest safe path from S to G that avoids all holes, and return the best and second-best safe paths as Python dictionaries mapping each visited state to its action, using None for the goal or holes.’</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">’
Figure </span><a href="#A7.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> compares MIRA under the original and alternative prompts. The learning curves and final returns are closely aligned, showing that MIRA’s performance is stable under natural variations in how the environment description is presented.</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">G.1.2 </span>Threshold Sensitivity</h4>

<figure id="A7.F14" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/rb_Sen.png" id="A7.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:242/120;" width="242" height="120" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span><span id="A7.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Sensitivity to the screening threshold. Lenient thresholds graft more candidate nodes into memory early, producing broader shaping during exploration but a slower overall improvement rate. Stricter thresholds delay graph growth yet yield sharper mid-training gains once high-confidence nodes appear. All settings converge to a narrow performance band.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">T</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">o assess the sensitivity of the screening rule, we conduct a study that varies the acceptance threshold while keeping the overall method fixed. The threshold, therefore, controls when and how densely the graph is populated, not whether shaping exists at all.
The main results of the paper uses </span><math id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=3</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> LLM completions, which was chosen for efficiency across all experiments. For this diagnostic test only, we set </span><math id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">k</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=4</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> to obtain cleaner fractional thresholds corresponding to meaningful agreement levels on the </span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Doorkey</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> environment. We evaluate three settings: a lenient majority rule (</span><math id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\geq 2/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">τ</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">≥</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">2</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\geq 2/4</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">), a stricter majority rule (</span><math id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\geq 3/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">τ</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">≥</mo><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">3</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">/</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">4</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\geq 3/4</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">), and unanimous agreement (</span><math id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">τ</mi><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">=</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=1</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).
</span><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">Figure <a href="#A7.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ G.1.2 Threshold Sensitivity ‣ G.1 Sensitivity and Robustness Studies ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows that the threshold primarily affects the early phase of learning.
With a lenient threshold, more candidate suggestions are grafted as healthy graph nodes and added to the memory. This leads the agent to receive utility bonuses on more states while it is still exploring. As a result, even if some early nodes may be slightly misaligned, the overall trend still pushes the agent toward regions that have higher returns. It is then up to the agent to correct those nodes through experience or increase their confidence if they turn out to be helpful, which explains why the overall improvement can be slower in this setting.
In the stricter settings, fewer suggestions pass the screening, so graph growth is delayed and the shaping signal remains sparse. Early learning progresses more slowly, but once these high-confidence nodes enter the graph, they produce larger and more coherent utility bonuses along trajectories that already correlate with high return, which creates the steeper rise visible in the mid-training region. The near-final performance still lies in a narrow band, since the shaping term is bounded and eventually dominated by the learned value function.
This behavior is consistent with the design of our utility-based shaping, using the LLM’s possibly imperfect but often still useful knowledge to accelerate the initial learning phase while ensuring stable progress as more reliable evidence accumulates.</span></p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Early Advantage Dynamics</h3>

<figure id="A7.F15" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/early_return.png" id="A7.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:247/134;" width="247" height="134" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>Return curves for different <math id="A7.F15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> values under fixed <math id="A7.F15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> settings. Markers indicate the first iteration where performance begins to diverge, signaling when <math id="A7.F15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> starts to meaningfully affect learning. Early on, the critic signal is weak, and <math id="A7.F15.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is driven mostly by the utility term. When <math id="A7.F15.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> is large enough, shaping accelerates the critic’s contribution by up to 50 iterations and leads to around 2.5× higher return compared to the unshaped case.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A7.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ G.2 Early Advantage Dynamics ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> provides empirical support for the central intuition behind our shaping formulation.
We plot return curves for each <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> group (color), across different <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> values (line style).
Early in training, return curves within each <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> group remain tightly clustered, indicating that <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the critic’s estimate, provides little useful signal, regardless of how it is weighted.
Divergence points, marked on the figure, denote the first iteration where the return spread across <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> values exceeds a certain threshold, signaling that <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> has begun contributing meaningfully to the shaped advantage <math id="A7.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}_{t}=\eta_{t}A_{t}+\xi_{t}U_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the absence of shaping (<math id="A7.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi=0</annotation></semantics></math>, gray lines), this occurs relatively late (iteration 131), whereas with shaping (<math id="A7.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>), it happens substantially earlier (iterations 81–113, depending on <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math>). This shows that the utility term not only supports early learning but also accelerates the emergence of a reliable critic. These results validate our choice to softly shape advantages, and emphasize the importance of carefully tuning <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A7.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>: insufficient shaping slows critic learning, which in turn leads to substantially lower mean returns.</p>
</div>
<section id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Remark (Optimization Landscape in Sparse-Reward Regimes).</h5>

<div id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In sparse-reward environments, standard policy gradient methods such as PPO may
exhibit near-zero expected gradients in early training, as reward-based
advantage estimates <math id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> are often uninformative until a successful trajectory
is observed.
The non-vanishing update result (Theorem <a href="#Thmthm1" title="Theorem 1 (Non-Vanishing Updates in Sparse-Reward Regimes). ‣ 2.4 Adaptive Advantage Shaping ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) implies that the
proposed shaping objective induces a consistent gradient signal
<math id="A7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{k}\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}[U]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>𝔼</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>U</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{k}\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}[U]</annotation></semantics></math> even when reward-based advantages are weak.
This additional structure modifies the local optimization landscape by providing
an informative descent direction derived from trajectory similarity, thereby
facilitating earlier and more stable optimization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.3 </span>Relative Wall Time</h3>

<figure id="A7.F16" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/wall.png" id="A7.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:274/151;" width="274" height="151" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>Wall-clock runtimes across environments. Time required to reach a 0.5 return (left): PPO reaches 0.5 only on <span id="A7.F16.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Frozen Lake</span>, while both MIRA variants converge across tasks. Runtime for 2k training steps (right): Online MIRA incurs extra overhead from initial LLM queries, but this cost reduces wasted exploration and leads to faster convergence in terms of overall wall time.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We measure relative wall-clock time as the end-to-end runtime per iteration to assess each method’s computational burden. Environments with a more complex step logic, such as <span id="A7.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span>, which involves door toggling, key collection, and distractor dynamics, incur higher per-step simulation costs.
Tasks like <span id="A7.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span> and <span id="A7.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LavaCrossing</span> further increase runtime through frequent failures that trigger repeated episode resets and buffer re-initializations. In contrast, <span id="A7.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Frozen Lake</span>’s tabular, low-dimensional transitions execute very quickly, so all methods complete rapidly (we do not run the online variant here since the offline approach suffices). Occasional LLM queries introduce network latency that further raises wall time in the slower domains. As a result, relative wall time grows with both the intrinsic simulation complexity of the environment and any additional algorithmic overhead (e.g., LLM calls).</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Relative Wall Time ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> reports wall-clock times for two measures: reaching a 0.5 return (left) and completing a 2k-step run (right). In the left panel, PPO reaches 0.5 only on <span id="A7.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Frozen Lake</span>, while both MIRA variants converge across all environments.
In the right panel, PPO shows the lowest per-step runtime because online MIRA incurs some additional cost from its initial LLM queries. However, early queries reduce wasted exploration, allowing online MIRA to reach 0.5 return much faster overall, yielding a net gain in efficiency despite the upfront overhead.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A <span id="A7.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">complete view of these trade-offs comes from considering both Figure <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Relative Wall Time ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> and the right-hand panel of Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Together, they show how higher return and wall-clock time interact when online LLM latency is present. Although online MIRA incurs additional latency from occasional queries, a substantial portion of this cost is offset by faster policy improvement: the agent spends less time in unproductive exploration and reaches competent behavior sooner. This can be seen directly by comparing the left and right panels of Figure <a href="#A7.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ G.3 Relative Wall Time ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>: online MIRA has slightly higher per-step runtime, yet it reaches the 0.5 return threshold earlier in wall-clock time. The right-hand panel of Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reinforces this result, showing that the higher cost of online queries is compensated by more rapid performance gains.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.4 </span>Memory Growth Analysis</h3>

<figure id="A7.F17" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:44%;"><img src="2602.17930v1/figs/mem_size1.png" id="A7.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:242/112;" width="242" height="112" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span><span id="A7.F17.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Memory size growth over training. Early growth is followed by convergence once trajectories become consistent, with final sizes increasing from <span id="A7.F17.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBall</span> to <span id="A7.F17.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> to <span id="A7.F17.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Distracted DoorKey</span> in line with task complexity.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A7.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">W</span><span id="A7.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">e examine how the memory graph evolves during training. MIRA updates the graph only when computing the utility term during advantage estimation, so memory expansion occurs once per training batch rather than at every environment step. Because batches contain full trajectories, their lengths vary across environments. To obtain a consistent summary across tasks, we record the memory size every 100 training iterations.</span><span id="A7.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">F</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">igure </span><a href="#A7.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ G.4 Memory Growth Analysis ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> reports memory growth for </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">RedBall</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">DoorKey</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, and </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Distracted DoorKey</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. In all three environments, memory grows quickly during early training, reflecting the period where the agent encounters diverse high-return segments and, when applicable, issues LLM queries that generate candidate memory additions.
As trajectories converge to a consistent solution, memory expansion slows and eventually stabilizes.
The plateau levels reflect the structural demands of each task: </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">RedBall</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> retains only a small set of nodes due to its simple subgoal structure, whereas </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">DoorKey</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> and </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Distracted DoorKey</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> require a richer collection of region-anchored segments. </span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.16" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Distracted DoorKey</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.17" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> ends up with the largest memory, as the distractor objects create additional path variants that help guide the agent, while the total size remains bounded and does not grow throughout later training.</span><span id="A7.SS4.p2.1.18" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.5 </span>Query Frequency Performance Summary</h3>

<div id="A7.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A7.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ G.5 Query Frequency Performance Summary ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> expands on Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in Subsection <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>. It shows how different online query budgets impact learning progress (SR90Return, indicating the mean return when success rate first exceeds 90%), final return, and convergence speed (total steps to termination). The results reinforce that while all MIRA variants outperform PPO, higher online budgets further accelerate training and improve asymptotic performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A7.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Performance on <span id="A7.T1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span>. SR90Return is the mean return when success rate first exceeds 90%; Final Return is the return at the end of training; Final Step is the total environment steps. MIRA variants outperform the baseline in both early and final return, with MIRA (large) achieving the highest values while converging fastest.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="A7.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.6 </span>MiniGrid Performance Summary</h3>

<div id="A7.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tables <a href="#A7.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ G.6 MiniGrid Performance Summary ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#A7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ G.6 MiniGrid Performance Summary ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> report detailed numerical results for all four MiniGrid tasks, including mean returns and success rates averaged over unseen seeds. MIRA consistently outperforms both PPO and the hierarchical baseline across all environments, including the more complex ones such as <span id="A7.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">DoorKey</span> and <span id="A7.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RedBlueDoor</span>. Welch’s t-tests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruxton, 2006</a>)</cite> show no statistically significant difference between MIRA and LLM4Teach at the 0.05 level across metrics and environments (Table <a href="#A7.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ G.6 MiniGrid Performance Summary ‣ Appendix G Extended Experimental Studies ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). These results support the aggregate performance trends in the main text (Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Tabular Benchmark and Partially Observable Tasks ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MIRA: Memory-Integrated Reinforcement Learning Agent with Limited LLM Guidance" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>), demonstrating that MIRA improves both final return and task completion.</p>
</div>
